notes.meaning: Israel arrived at the Sinai desert at the start of the third month, about seven weeks after leaving Egypt. This timing matches what later became the feast of Pentecost, celebrated fifty days after Passover. God led His people to this rugged region at the exact time He had planned.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: The word translated as wilderness refers to open grazing land used by herders, rather than an empty sea of sand dunes.

notes.meaning: After journeying from Rephidim, the people set up camp in front of Mount Sinai. Reaching this mountain fulfilled the promise God gave Moses at the burning bush that Israel would worship Him on this very ground. Israel remained camped at this site for about a year while receiving the law and building the tabernacle.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars and explorers propose that Mount Sinai was located in northwestern Saudi Arabia rather than the traditional site in the southern Sinai Peninsula.

notes.meaning: Moses climbed up the mountain to meet with God, and the Lord called out to him. God addressed the people as both the house of Jacob and the sons of Israel. The name Jacob recalled their humble, weak family roots, while Israel pointed to what God had made them into as a chosen nation.

The Lord told Moses to remind the people of how He had defeated Egypt and rescued them. He pictured their escape as being carried on eagles' wings, like a parent eagle carrying its young safely on its back. Most importantly, God rescued them so He could bring them close to Himself.

God offered Israel a covenant, which is a sacred, binding agreement between God and His people. If they listened to His voice and kept this agreement, they would be His special, treasured possession out of all the nations. Even though the entire world belongs to God, He chose to pour special love upon Israel.

differ.view: The covenant at Sinai is part of the unfolding covenant of grace, showing a people who were already redeemed how to live in obedience to God.
The condition of obedience here marks a distinct age of law, where blessing depended on human performance unlike the unconditional grace of the new covenant.

notes.meaning: God promised that Israel would be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, set apart completely for His service. In other nations only a few special men served as priests, but all Israel was invited to have direct access to God and show His truth to the world. The New Testament uses these same words to describe Christian believers as a royal priesthood.

Moses came down the mountain and gathered the elders, who were the respected leaders of each tribe. He clearly explained everything the Lord had said so they could share it with the whole camp. Moses gave the people a genuine choice to accept or decline God's offer.

The people answered with one voice, promising to do everything the Lord commanded. Moses then took their reply back up the mountain to God. The people answered with sincere willingness, though they did not yet understand how hard it would be to keep God's perfect law.

The Lord announced that He would speak from a dense cloud so the people could hear Him talking with Moses. The cloud hid God's blinding majesty while giving unmistakable proof that Moses was His chosen messenger. Because the people heard God speak directly, they learned to trust Moses' leadership for generations to come.

God told Moses to consecrate the people over the next two days and have them wash their clothes. To consecrate means to set someone or something apart as holy for God. Washing their outer garments was a physical reminder to clean their hearts from sin through repentance before meeting God.

The people were told to be ready by the third day, when the Lord would come down on Mount Sinai in plain view of everyone. Requiring two full days of preparation showed that human unworthiness before God cannot be washed away in a hurry. Though Israel would see no physical shape of God, they would witness undeniable signs of His glory.

Moses was told to place a boundary around the mountain so no one would touch its base or try to climb it. God warned that anyone who touched the mountain would be put to death. This strict line taught the people deep reverence and showed that sinners cannot casually walk into God's holy presence.

Anyone who crossed the line was not to be seized by hand, but put to death from a distance with stones or arrows. Laying a hand on the guilty person would require crossing the boundary and sharing in the offense. Only when the ram's horn sounded a long, final blast were the people permitted to draw near to the mountain's base.

Moses climbed down from the mountain and guided the people in their preparations. The Israelites obeyed the Lord's instructions and washed their garments. Cleansing their clothes helped turn their attention away from everyday chores and focus on the holy God.

Moses told the camp to be ready for the third day and to pause normal marital relations during this time. While marriage is pure and lawful, setting aside ordinary pleasures helped the people focus entirely on prayer and spiritual readiness. They needed undivided attention as they waited to meet their King.

On the morning of the third day, loud thunder crashed and lightning flashed around a dark, heavy cloud resting on the mountain. A heavenly ram's horn blew with a piercing blast that shook the camp and made everyone tremble. These terrifying signs displayed God's majesty and the absolute seriousness of His law.

Moses led the trembling people out of their camp to the foot of Mount Sinai to meet with God. They stopped at the base of the mountain, right at the boundary line God had marked out. Even though the sight was terrifying, God was drawing His people near so they could hear Him speak.

Mount Sinai was completely covered in smoke because the Lord came down on it in fire. The smoke rose into the air like the plume of an enormous furnace, and the entire mountain shook violently. These powerful signs showed that God is a consuming fire against sin and that creation trembles before Him.

As the sound of the horn grew louder and louder, Moses spoke, and God answered him with a voice in the thunder. The horn served as a royal announcement, calling the entire nation to silence. God answered Moses out loud so everyone would know that Moses truly spoke with divine authority.

The Lord descended to the summit of Mount Sinai and summoned Moses to come up. Moses obeyed and climbed to the top into the midst of the smoke and cloud. Even while the mountain shook with power, Moses showed trust in God by going up to meet Him.

The moment Moses reached the top, the Lord sent him back down to warn the people not to push past the boundary. God knew that curiosity might tempt people to gaze at His glory, which would result in their death. His presence is so holy that sinners cannot approach Him on their own terms.

The Lord commanded that even the priests who drew near to Him must consecrate themselves, or He would strike them down. These priests were likely family heads or elders who offered sacrifices before the official priesthood of Aaron was set up. Having an honored title did not exempt anyone from the need for deep reverence and cleansing.

Moses answered that the people could not come up because the mountain had already been marked off with boundaries and declared holy. Moses assumed that the earlier warning and the physical barrier would be enough to keep everyone back. He thought the people would naturally obey, but God knew human curiosity and weakness far better than Moses did.

The Lord told Moses to hurry back down and bring Aaron up with him later. He repeated that neither the priests nor the people were allowed to push past the barrier, lest God break out against them in judgment. No position or crowd had permission to cross the lines God had established.

Moses obeyed the Lord, walked down the mountain, and repeated the warning to the people. He instructed them to stay behind the line and prepare to receive God's words. By delivering this charge, Moses kept the camp safe right before God spoke the Ten Commandments.
